stem: At intake, a consultant working online with Talia, a collegiate fencer, had her complete the Test of Performance Strategies. Twelve weeks later, wanting something shorter, the consultant gave her the Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 instead. Talia's ACSI-28 coping-with-adversity score looks high next to her intake TOPS emotional-control score. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Treat the higher score as tentative progress and confirm it at the next check-in
Convert each score to a percentile using its own norms, then compare the two
Re-administer the TOPS so change is judged on the same measure, with other data
Adopt the ACSI-28 from here on and treat this score as her new starting point
rationales: Calling it tentative still treats two different instruments as one yardstick. The subscales measure related but different constructs on different scales, so there is no 'progress' to confirm.

Percentiles put each score on its own norm group's scale, but they still describe different constructs from different instruments (and possibly different norm samples), so the comparison remains invalid.

Best answer. Judging change requires the same (or an established parallel) measure under comparable conditions. Re-administering the intake instrument and corroborating with other sources — her report, coach observation, bout data — gives a defensible picture of change.
Switching to a new baseline is reasonable for future monitoring, but it abandons the comparison with intake that the reassessment is meant to provide.
takeaway: To show change, repeat the same measure under comparable conditions and triangulate; scores from different instruments can't be compared, even as percentiles.

stem: An esports organization hired a consultant to run a four-week communication program for its five-player roster. End-of-session ratings were uniformly positive. The general manager now asks whether the players actually communicate differently during competition. Which evaluation step best answers that question?
options: Interview players about which parts of the program they found most useful
Give the players a short quiz on the communication model they were taught
Code recorded voice comms from matches before and after for the trained behaviors
Compare the team's tournament placings for the seasons before and after
rationales: Asking what players found useful gathers reaction-level information (Kirkpatrick level 1) and opinions about value, not evidence of whether their in-match communication changed.
A quiz assesses learning (knowledge of the model), Kirkpatrick's second level. Players can know the model without using it under competitive pressure.

Best choice. The manager's question is about behavior transfer — Kirkpatrick's third level. Systematically coding the specific trained behaviors (e.g., concise callouts, confirmations) in match recordings before and after the program measures whether the skills are used where it matters.
Placings are a results-level outcome influenced by roster changes, opponents, game patches and many other factors, so they can't show whether communication itself changed.
takeaway: Match the evaluation level to the question: reaction and learning don't show transfer — observe the targeted behavior in the performance setting.
